findings.title: Turnaround time improved while traffic grew
findings.inference: Average turnaround moved from 61h to 66h while monthly calls grew ~38% — throughput scaled without eroding vessel service time.

findings.title: Pre-berthing waits above 24h concentrate at a few terminals
findings.inference: A persistent tail of calls waits more than a day for a berth. The wait is not uniform — it concentrates where cargo mix meets berth compatibility limits, so berth-window planning (not dredging or capex) is the first lever.

findings.title: Berth-on-arrival service level
findings.inference: The share of vessels berthed within six hours of arrival is the customer-facing service number agents quote; lifting it is mostly a scheduling discipline gain.

findings.title: Terminal risk ranking (trailing 12 months)
findings.inference: One composite number per terminal — incident intensity, congestion and compliance blended — driving the twin's colour and the ranking list.

findings.title: Volume and risk are different lists
findings.inference: The busiest terminal is not the riskiest — targeting attention by volume alone would miss where incidents and congestion actually cluster.

findings.title: Incident intensity and the near-miss ratio
findings.inference: A healthy safety culture reports many near-misses per serious event (Heinrich ratio). Track this number monthly: a falling near-miss ratio with steady severity means under-reporting, not improvement.

findings.title: Oil-sheen / spill events by year
findings.inference: Tier-1 sheen events cluster around bunkering and hose work at the liquid berths; each carries GPCB notification duty. The trend line, not any single event, is the regulator conversation.

findings.title: Equipment-failure incidents by year
findings.inference: Crane, gangway and conveyor failures are the largest single incident class — the maintenance-planning conversation belongs in the same room as HSE.

findings.title: Traffic trajectory by terminal

evidence.note: [terminal, latest monthly calls, trend calls/yr, volatility]

findings.inference: Where the next year's traffic pressure lands if trends hold — the berth-window and manning plan should be built against these slopes, not last year's average.

findings.title: Berth occupancy headroom
findings.inference: Every terminal sits below the UNCTAD 40-70% congestion band — the port can absorb its own growth trend for years before berth capacity binds; marketing, not construction, is the growth constraint.

findings.title: What moves with terminal risk
findings.inference: Correlates of the composite: congestion and incident intensity dominate; raw volume alone is a weak predictor of risk.

findings.title: Terminal typologies (k-means, 3 clusters)
findings.inference: Data-driven segmentation: high-volume container quays, steady bulk berths, and the low-frequency/high-consequence liquid & offshore group each need a different operating playbook.

findings.title: Mundra vs Indian major-port averages
findings.inference: The credibility yardstick: berth-day output runs ~3x the major-port average (mechanised terminals), turnaround is competitive, and the PSC detention rate sits near the regional MoU norm — the one number to watch, not celebrate.

findings.title: Collections vs the 95% target
findings.inference: Cumulative collection efficiency against the commercial target, with the outstanding book in crore — the number the CFO reads first; the terminal-level split shows which agents' books drive the receivable.

findings.title: Outstanding receivables by terminal
findings.inference: Where the receivable concentrates; pair with the agent directory for the collection call list.
